items.followUp: Who first observed crossing over, and in which organism and year?

rubric.why: Identifies when crossing over was discovered.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct year.

rubric.why: Identifies the scientist who discovered crossing over in Drosophila.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct scientist.

modelAnswer: Crossing over in Drosophila melanogaster was discovered by Thomas Hunt Morgan in 1911.

items.followUp: Define crossing over and name the scientist who first observed it.

rubric.why: A definition of mitosis must identify it as nuclear division.
rubric.description: Defines mitosis as division of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying nuclear division.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces two nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent nucleus.
rubric.description: States that mitosis forms two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number.

modelAnswer: Mitosis is the division of a cell nucleus into two daughter nuclei, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.

items.followUp: Define a chromosome and state one function of the mitotic spindle.

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme action through the fit between the substrate and the enzyme's active site.
rubric.description: Explains that a substrate with a complementary shape fits the enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complementary fit or formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model.
rubric.description: Names Emil Fischer as the proposer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct name.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, a substrate with a shape complementary to an enzyme’s active site fits into it, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The model was proposed by Emil Fischer.

items.followUp: Who coined the term “enzyme,” and in what year?

rubric.why: Identifies the year the term was first used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct year.

rubric.why: Identifies the scientist who first used the term enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct scientist.

modelAnswer: The term “enzyme” was first used by Wilhelm Kühne in 1878.

items.followUp: What is chemical energy, and how is it stored in living organisms?

rubric.why: Kinetic energy is one of the two main forms of energy in living organisms.
rubric.description: Defines kinetic energy as energy of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct form and definition.

rubric.why: Potential energy is energy stored due to position or structure.
rubric.description: Defines potential energy as stored energy due to position or structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct form and definition.

modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, such as the movement of an organism or its parts.
Potential energy is stored energy due to an object's position or structure.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis as light intensity increases?

rubric.why: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration raises the rate of photosynthesis when carbon dioxide is limiting.
rubric.description: States that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the positive effect of increased carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: The increase does not continue indefinitely; another limiting factor eventually restricts the rate.
rubric.description: States that the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the limit or plateau.

modelAnswer: As carbon dioxide concentration increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases while carbon dioxide is a limiting factor.
The rate eventually levels off when another factor limits photosynthesis.

items.followUp: State two factors that increase the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Evaporation of water from leaf cells creates tension or suction in the xylem.
rubric.description: Gives water evaporation or loss from the leaves as a cause of transpirational pull.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying evaporation or water loss from leaves.

rubric.why: Cohesion between water molecules, and adhesion to xylem walls, helps transmit the pull through the water column.
rubric.description: Gives cohesion between water molecules or adhesion to xylem walls as a cause.

modelAnswer: Evaporation of water from the leaf cells during transpiration creates tension in the xylem.
Cohesion between water molecules helps transmit this pull along the continuous water column.

items.followUp: How does wind affect the rate of transpiration?

rubric.why: A rise in temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and thus increases transpiration.
rubric.description: States that higher temperature increases the rate of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of rising temperature.

rubric.why: A fall in temperature reduces evaporation and lowers the rate of transpiration.
rubric.description: States that lower temperature decreases the rate of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of falling temperature.

modelAnswer: A rise in temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces, so the rate of transpiration increases.
A fall in temperature reduces evaporation, so the rate of transpiration decreases.
